Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

CANNES, France (CNN) -- After eleven days, hundreds of screenings and thousands of snaps from the paparazzi, there could only be one Palme d'Or winner. Austrian director Michael Haneke hugs the president of the Cannes jury, French actress Isabelle Huppert. "The White Ribbon," by Austrian director Michael Haneke, was awarded the prize for its depiction of the cruel punishments meted out at a rural German school before the First World War. "The Palme d'Or is the best prize a filmmaker can win," said Haneke at a press conference following his award. "I am not proud, but I am very happy. In my opinion, it's silly to be proud." It was a case of fifth time lucky for Haneke, who has previously been nominated for the award for "Funny Games" (1997), "Code Unknown" (2000), "The Piano Teacher" (2001) and "Hidden" (2005). "There are always rumors at the festival, and one must not take them seriously," the director said. "When I presented "Hidden" [in 2005], everyone was telling me I was going to win the Palme. And I didn't get it." Jury president Isabelle Huppert, the French actress who won the best actress prize at the 2001 festival for "The Piano Teacher," said she was delighted to have the chance to honor her former director. "I think I always loved him as a director, and that's why I've worked with him before," she said at the post-awards press conference. "To me, the movie is very philosophical. And his style, and his direction are totally ethical in my mind. That's what I wanted to reward." The American actress Robin Wright Penn, who also sat on the festival jury, laughed off rumors that the decision was hotly disputed. "There have been rumors circulating that we were fighting in the room," she told the press conference. "The beauty about loving each other ... [is that] we could disagree, and we still love each other. I felt like we built a consensus among us," she said. "It was like being on "Big Brother," except you could go to the movies," added British screenwriter and fellow juror Hanif Kureishi. "Some of the films are very long," he joked. Elsewhere, Charlotte Gainsbourg won the best actress prize for her shocking turn in Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," featuring scenes of genital mutilation that left audiences stunned. Christolph Waltz won best actor for his role in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," while Brillante Mendoza secured the best director gong for "Kinatay." The jury prize was shared by Korean auteur Park Chan-Wook's vampire film "Thirst," and Andrea Arnold's "Fish Tank," while the grand prix went to "The Prophet," by director Jacques Audiard.

While the jury did not disclose vote totals, its decision was greeted as a major endorsement for a film that had been among the most discussed titles of the competition.

Haneke, whose earlier films include **“Caché,” “The Piano Teacher”** and **“Funny Games,”** accepted the award with characteristic restraint, thanking the festival, his collaborators and the actors who helped bring the stark ensemble drama to the screen.

Other major prizes went to some of the festival’s most prominent contenders:

- **Grand Prix:** **“A Prophet”** by French director **Jacques Audiard**, a prison crime drama that emerged as one of the best-reviewed films in competition.  
- **Best Director:** **Brillante Mendoza** for **“Kinatay,”** a grim Philippine thriller that divided critics but impressed the jury with its raw intensity.  
- **Best Actor:** **Christoph Waltz** for his breakout performance as Nazi officer Col. Hans Landa in Quentin Tarantino’s **“Inglourious Basterds.”**  
- **Best Actress:** **Charlotte Gainsbourg** for Lars von Trier’s controversial **“Antichrist.”**  
- **Jury Prize:** Shared by **Andrea Arnold’s “Fish Tank”** and **Park Chan-wook’s “Thirst.”**

- **Camera d’Or:** **“Samson & Delilah,”** from Australian director **Warwick Thornton**, honoring the best first feature.  
- **Short Film Palme d’Or:** **“Arena,”** directed by **João Salaviza**.

The awards capped a Cannes edition marked by high-profile auteurs, provocative films and sharp critical debate. But in the end, the festival’s top honor went to Haneke’s chilling historical parable — a film whose quiet surfaces conceal deep social and psychological unease.

**CANNES, France —** Michael Haneke’s austere black-and-white drama **“The White Ribbon”** won the **Palme d’Or**, the Cannes Film Festival’s top prize, at a closing ceremony that capped nearly two weeks of red carpets, fierce debate and a competition lineup heavy with political unease and moral ambiguity.

The German-language film, set in a Protestant village in northern Germany on the eve of World War I, was honored Sunday night by a jury led by French actress **Isabelle Huppert**, who praised the film’s “rigor, mystery and moral force.” The award marked a crowning moment for Haneke, long regarded as one of European cinema’s most uncompromising directors.

Accepting the Palme d’Or, Haneke appeared visibly moved but characteristically restrained.

> “I am very happy — and very grateful,” Haneke said from the stage. “This film was made with great seriousness by everyone involved. It belongs to the actors, to the crew, and to the producers who believed that a difficult film could still find an audience.”

“The White Ribbon” explores a series of disturbing incidents in a tightly controlled village, gradually suggesting the roots of authoritarianism, repression and violence. Shot in luminous monochrome, the film had emerged during the festival as one of the critical favorites, admired for its precision and unsettled atmosphere.

Huppert, who had worked with Haneke on “The Piano Teacher” and “Time of the Wolf,” said the jury’s decision reflected both the film’s artistic command and its wider resonance.

> “It is a film that does not explain everything, and that is part of its power,” Huppert said backstage. “It asks where violence begins — in families, in schools, in silence, in obedience. That question stayed with all of us.”

Jury members said the deliberations were serious but ultimately clear.

> “We saw many strong films, but Haneke’s film had a rare authority,” one juror said. “Every frame felt necessary. It is historical, but it speaks very directly to the present.”

Another jury member described the Palme winner as “beautiful, severe and unforgettable,” adding:

> “It does what great cinema can do — it makes the audience uncomfortable in a way that is productive.”

The evening’s other major awards reflected the breadth of the competition. **Jacques Audiard’s “A Prophet”** won the **Grand Prix**, the festival’s second-highest honor, for its muscular prison saga about a young inmate’s rise through the criminal underworld. The **Best Director** prize went to **Brillante Mendoza** for **“Kinatay,”** while the **Jury Prize** was shared by **Andrea Arnold’s “Fish Tank”** and **Park Chan-wook’s “Thirst.”**

Acting honors went to **Christoph Waltz**, named **Best Actor** for his breakout performance as the chillingly charismatic Nazi officer Hans Landa in Quentin Tarantino’s **“Inglourious Basterds,”** and **Charlotte Gainsbourg**, who won **Best Actress** for her harrowing role in Lars von Trier’s **“Antichrist.”**

Still, the night belonged to Haneke.

For years, the Austrian director has been a Cannes regular, known for films that scrutinize guilt, cruelty, spectatorship and social order. “The White Ribbon” continues that inquiry on a broader historical canvas, depicting children, parents, clergy and landowners bound together by fear, discipline and suspicion.

Speaking later to reporters, Haneke said he did not view the film as a simple explanation of fascism, but rather as a study of conditions that allow extremism to take root.

> “I do not make films to give answers,” he said. “I try to pose questions as precisely as possible. If the film suggests that humiliation and repression can produce violence, then that is something each viewer must think about.”

Asked whether he expected such a severe work to receive the festival’s highest honor, Haneke smiled.

> “One never expects the Palme d’Or,” he said. “At Cannes, you hope the film is seen seriously. Tonight, it has been.”

The ceremony, held inside the Palais des Festivals, brought the 62nd Cannes Film Festival to a close with the usual mixture of glamour and tension. But the selection of “The White Ribbon” gave the evening a sober final note — a reminder that Cannes often reserves its highest praise for films willing to confront history, discomfort and the darker corners of human behavior.

As Huppert put it:

> “The Palme d’Or is not only for beauty. It is for cinema that remains with us after the lights come up. ‘The White Ribbon’ is such a film.”

The **Jury Prize** was shared by two films: British director Andrea Arnold’s coming-of-age drama **“Fish Tank”** and South Korean filmmaker Park Chan-wook’s vampire tale **“Thirst.”**
